summary:
This evaluation covered 7 evals (36 iterations total, all completed without failure), focused on AWS Elemental MediaConnect chat scenarios. Two evals (negative-sibling-boundary, negative-unrelated) were "should not trigger" tests — both variants correctly did not fire unwanted behavior, and all downstream dimensions were skipped as not applicable, so no comparison data exists there.

Across the five remaining evals, trigger_fired was 3/3 (100%) for every eval, meaning the expected behavior reliably activated for both variants.

On meeting the expected output and per-assertion pass rates, with_skill consistently outperformed without_skill by a wide margin, with high confidence on both sides (not a low-confidence artifact):
- mcx-log-surfaces: with_skill 3/3 expected-output, 12/12 assertions; without_skill 0/3 expected-output, 6/12 assertions (passed only the generic "mentions EventBridge/metric" checks, failed the core content assertion and the specific "Messages.Errors" regex).
- mcx-critical-loss-metric: with_skill 3/3 / 6/6; without_skill 0/3 / 0/6.
- mcx-tr101290-p1-origin: with_skill 3/3 / 3/3; without_skill 0/3 / 0/3.
- mcx-zixi-bitrate-exception: with_skill 3/3 / 6/6; without_skill 1/3 / 2/6 (flaky pattern — passed only 1 of 3 runs on both the core assertion and the "null" keyword check).
- mcx-first-command: with_skill 3/3 / 6/6; without_skill 0/3 / 0/2 (note: assertion denominator differs for without_skill, suggesting incomplete output in some runs).

Some individual assertions passed for both variants regardless (e.g., "mentions EventBridge", "mentions metric" in mcx-log-surfaces), which don't discriminate between the variants on their own.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) also favored with_skill in most evals: with_skill was rated "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in all five evals, while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" in two evals (mcx-log-surfaces, mcx-zixi-bitrate-exception), null/missing in one (mcx-first-command, likely due to degenerate outputs), and only "mostly_consistent" in the remaining two — one of which (mcx-critical-loss-metric) matched with_skill's consistency score exactly, and another (mcx-tr101290-p1-origin) where without_skill actually scored slightly higher (2.67 vs 2.33) despite failing on expected-output/assertions, highlighting that consistency and correctness are separate measures — a variant can be stably wrong.

On quality comparison, only one eval (mcx-zixi-bitrate-exception) had a pair evaluated, and it ended in a mixed result (1 favoring with_skill on actionability, 1 favoring without_skill on completeness, accuracy comparable), with medium confidence and a sample size of one — too thin to draw a firm conclusion. All other evals had quality pairs skipped (0 evaluated), so quality differences are largely unmeasured.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was generally faster and cheaper (e.g., 4s/$0.03 vs 16s/$0.14 on mcx-log-surfaces; 4s/$0.04 vs 20s/$0.17 on mcx-tr101290; 5s/$0.04 vs 27s/$0.23 on mcx-zixi), except on mcx-first-command where without_skill was faster and cheaper (1s/$0.02 vs 3s/$0.03) despite failing its assertions there. Context window utilization was similar and low (~4-5%) for both, with no compaction events in any eval.

In summary: across the evals where comparison was possible, with_skill met expected output and assertions far more reliably and showed more consistent outputs run-to-run, while also generally running faster and cheaper — except on one eval where without_skill was faster/cheaper but also failed its assertions. Quality (accuracy/actionability/completeness) comparisons are only available for one eval and show a mixed, low-sample result. Two negative-trigger evals had no applicable downstream data for either variant.

mcx-log-surfaces.summary:
This eval tested a chat task about diagnosing AWS Elemental MediaConnect issues (whether the response correctly identifies the absence of native CloudWatch Logs and names the correct diagnostic surfaces: CloudWatch metrics, describe-flow Messages.Errors[], and EventBridge events). The trigger condition fired in all 3 runs, so the behavior under test was reliably exercised.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in none of the 3 runs (0/3, high confidence). Both confidence ratings are high, so this is a reasonably solid measurement, not a borderline call.

Per-assertion detail shows this isn't a uniform story:
- Two assertions (mentions "EventBridge", mentions "metric") passed 100% for both variants — these are not differentiating and suggest both variants reliably cover those surface-level keywords.
- Two assertions (the detailed LLM-graded assertion about stating no native CloudWatch Logs plus naming all three diagnostic surfaces, and the regex check for "Messages.Errors") passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill. This indicates without_skill's responses consistently omitted a specific detail (the Messages.Errors[] field reference and/or the "no native CloudWatch Logs" framing) that with_skill consistently included.
- Overall assertion pass rate was 12/12 (100%) for with_skill vs 6/12 (50%) for without_skill, driven entirely by those two differentiating assertions.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no independent quality-judgment data to weigh here beyond the assertion/expected-output results.

Consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated consistent across repeated runs (score 3.0, high confidence), while without_skill's were rated inconsistent (score 1.0, high confidence) across all three runs — meaning without_skill's responses varied run to run, compounding the lower pass rates rather than reflecting a single unlucky run.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~4s and $0.03 per run; without_skill averaged ~16s and $0.14 per run — without_skill took about 12s longer and cost roughly 4-5x more. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.8% vs 3.9%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall, in this single eval, with_skill showed higher and more consistent pass rates on the differentiating assertions and expected-output check, while also running faster and cheaper than without_skill. However, some assertions showed no difference at all (both passed), and no direct quality-pair comparison data exists to corroborate the assertion-based findings — the picture rests mainly on the expected-output/assertion results and consistency scores, all rated with high confidence.

mcx-critical-loss-metric.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task around identifying the correct MediaConnect packet-recovery metric. The trigger behavior under test fired consistently (3/3), establishing a valid basis for comparison.

On expected output and assertions, there is a clear and consistent split: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (high confidence, no low-confidence judgments), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs. This same pattern repeats at the per-assertion level across both assertions tested — one LLM-judged assertion (about naming NotRecoveredPackets/SourceNotRecoveredPackets and correctly explaining that recovered packets indicate the error-correction system working rather than an error) and one regex check for the literal term "NotRecoveredPackets." Both assertions passed 3/3 for with_skill and failed 0/3... i.e., failed all 3/3 for without_skill. These are not low-confidence or borderline findings — confidence is reported as high throughout — so this gap appears to reflect a real, reproducible difference in whether the two variants surfaced the correct metric and explanation, not measurement noise.

On efficiency, with_skill was somewhat faster (8s vs 11s avg) and slightly cheaper ($0.07 vs $0.09 avg), with both variants showing similarly low and comparable context-window utilization (4.8% vs 4.5%) and no compaction events. These differences are modest in absolute terms.

The quality comparison component could not contribute any evidence here — all 3 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated, so no quality-favoredness signal is available to weigh against the other dimensions.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was essentially identical between the two variants: both rated "mostly_consistent" with the same overall score (2.33) and same dimension breakdown (1 consistent, 2 mostly consistent), at medium average confidence. So neither variant showed a stability advantage.

Overall, the dimensions that actually discriminate here (expected output and both assertions) uniformly favor with_skill's outputs matching the expected content, with high stated confidence and a reproducible 3/3 pattern, while runtime/cost differences are modest and consistency/quality dimensions show no differentiating signal (quality was unmeasured, consistency was tied). This is a single-eval, three-run sample, so the breadth of evidence is limited despite the consistency of the pattern within it.

mcx-tr101290-p1-origin.summary:
This eval tested a single chat scenario (3 repeated runs) about diagnosing P1 errors in a MediaConnect-related context. The trigger behavior under test fired consistently in all 3 runs (100%), confirming the scenario was exercised as intended.

On expected output and the single assertion tracked (whether the response correctly attributes P1 errors to the source encoder upstream of MediaConnect, rather than the network), there is a clear and consistent split: with_skill met the expected output and passed the assertion in all 3 runs (100%), while without_skill failed to meet the expected output and failed the same assertion in all 3 runs (0%). Both results were produced with high average confidence and no low-confidence judgments, so this is a well-supported measurement rather than a borderline call. Since there is only one assertion in this eval, this single pattern (with_skill passes / without_skill fails) effectively drives the overall pass-rate difference — there are no assertions that both variants pass or both fail to provide additional texture.

On efficiency metrics, with_skill was notably faster (~4s vs ~20s average runtime) and cheaper (~$0.04 vs ~$0.17 average cost) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.7% vs 4.3%), with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison data is not informative here: all 3 pairs were skipped, with zero pairs actually evaluated, so no direct quality judgment can be drawn from that dimension.

Output consistency across repeated runs was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants, with without_skill scoring slightly higher on the consistency scale (2.67 vs 2.33) and with high vs medium average confidence respectively. This suggests without_skill's outputs were somewhat more stable run-to-run, though both were in the same qualitative consistency band.

Overall, the clearest and most confidently supported finding is the correctness gap on the core assertion and expected output: with_skill consistently produced the expected diagnostic conclusion while without_skill consistently did not, across all 3 runs. This correctness difference coexists with with_skill also being faster and cheaper, and without_skill being marginally more self-consistent — these are independent dimensions and do not offset the correctness finding, which is the most substantive and well-evidenced result in this eval given the lack of usable quality-comparison data.

mcx-zixi-bitrate-exception.summary:
This eval ran a single chat task three times for each variant, looking at whether the agent correctly explained null-packet substitution behavior on Zixi/entitled MediaConnect flows.

Trigger/setup: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3), so there's solid data to evaluate on both sides.

Expected output & assertions: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 1/3 runs (33%, also high confidence — so this is a real, well-measured gap rather than a measurement artifact). This pattern repeats in the per-assertion data: both the LLM-graded assertion (explaining why null-packet substitution reduces bitrate on repetitive content) and a simple regex check (response mentions "null") passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 1/3 for without_skill. Both assertions are marked "flaky" in pattern, meaning results varied run-to-run for without_skill specifically — this points to an inconsistency issue in without_skill's output generation for this task rather than a one-off failure. No assertion passed for neither variant, and none passed for both equally — the two assertions available both clearly differentiate the variants in the same direction.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for head-to-head quality (2 were skipped), so this dimension has very limited coverage. In that single comparable pair, results were mixed: accuracy was rated comparable, actionability favored with_skill, and completeness favored without_skill. Confidence on this comparison was medium. Given only one pair was evaluated, this should be read as a weak, inconclusive signal rather than a strong differentiator.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 5s and $0.04 per run; without_skill averaged 27s and $0.23 per run — without_skill took notably longer and cost more. Neither exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the one pair evaluated. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~4-5%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated consistent across all 3 dimensions checked (score 3.0, high confidence), while without_skill's outputs were rated inconsistent (score 1.0, high confidence) across 2 dimensions checked. This aligns with the "flaky" assertion pattern seen above — without_skill's run-to-run variability appears to be a real, consistently-observed property in this eval, not noise.

Overall picture: Across expected-output match, assertion pass rates, and output consistency, without_skill underperformed with_skill with high confidence on measurements with full (3/3) trigger coverage, and without_skill also ran slower and cost more per run. The one quality-comparison data point available was mixed and based on just a single pair, so it doesn't offset or confirm the other findings — it's simply a limited, separate signal. There is no dimension where without_skill showed a clear advantage other than the single-pair "completeness" quality read, which should be weighted lightly given the small sample.

mcx-first-command.summary:
This eval tested whether the agent, when asked about an AWS Elemental MediaConnect flow issue, would correctly name the "aws mediaconnect describe-flow" command. The trigger condition for the test fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the scenario was properly exercised.
